about: The Jev question sets the authoring tools beside this file ask while a plan is written (ask.ts, gate_jev.ts, jev_checks.ts, through jev.ts's loadQuestions), moved here from factory/questions.json so each file has one reader (#1449). Each set says when it is asked (`when`), who reads it (`reader`), how to turn it off (`rollback`), the keys its reader sends (`state`), where it came from (`provenance`) and whether its readings are calibrated; thresholds live in policy.json beside this file. A question is literal: it names no policy word, and nothing here decides anything. A Jev `null` routes that reading to the set's stated rollback, never to a guess. A reworded question is a different question: its readings mean something else.

authoring_ambiguity.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Could `sentences[i]` describe two apps that behave differently in a way the person who wrote `ask` would care about?
instructions.context: `ask` is everything the person wrote; `sentences` are its sentences, in order.

criteria.true: Two reasonable readings lead to apps that act differently
criteria.false: Every reasonable reading leads to the same behaviour

authoring_coherence.when: At jev_checks.ts --stage bundle; one_need also at --stage map
authoring_coherence.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

one_need.instructions: Does `piece.purpose` state one need that a single short sentence covers?

criteria.false: Two or more needs joined together

same_people.instructions: Do all of `piece.actions` serve the same people for the same reason?

criteria.true: The same people, the same reason
criteria.false: Some actions serve different people or a different reason

authoring_near_miss.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

instructions.question: If the app behaved like `near_miss` instead, would `story` still come out exactly as it is written?
instructions.context: `story` is the main story that should prove `piece` works; `story_steps` are its steps, each an action called (`tool`, `args`) and what the person then sees (`see`). `near_miss` is a look-alike that must fail it.

criteria.true: The story cannot tell the two apart
criteria.false: The story would come out differently for the look-alike

authoring_content_branch.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Does the action named `actions[i].name` in `store_module` behave differently depending on the wording of text the person typed, beyond whether it is empty?
instructions.context: `store_module` is the app's whole store code; `actions` are its actions, each with the piece it belongs to and its description. An action that treats a title ending in '?' differently is the kind of thing asked about.

criteria.true: It inspects the words and changes behaviour
criteria.false: It stores or compares the text without reading its wording

authoring_redundancy.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

same_need.instructions: Do `pieces[i].purpose` and `pieces[j].purpose` describe the same need?

authoring_surprise.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Would the person who wrote `ask` be surprised to learn that the app `assumption`?
instructions.context: `ask` is everything the person wrote; `assumption` is something the author assumed the app does, about what it does, who uses it or how it looks.

criteria.true: They would be surprised; it goes beyond or against what they asked
criteria.false: It is what they would expect from what they asked

authoring_map.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Is `piece.purpose` part of the core of what `summary` describes, rather than an extra?
instructions.context: `summary` says what the product is, why it exists and how it is used. `piece.purpose` is one thing the product could do; `other_purposes` are the other things it could do; `audience` are the people who use it.

instructions.question: Does `piece.purpose` serve what `summary` says the product is for?
instructions.context: `summary` says what the product is, why it exists and how it is used. `other_purposes` are the other things the product could do.

authoring_decompose.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Could `audience` use `plan` on its own and judge whether it works?
instructions.context: `summary` says what the whole product is. `plan` is one part of it: its title and the things it lets people do. `built_before` are the parts built before it, in order, which `audience` already has.

criteria.true: Usable and judgeable on its own
criteria.false: Nothing to use or judge until other parts exist

authoring_gate.when: At each proof-gate round, beside the agent reader
authoring_gate.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Does `clauses[i].text` state a computable fact: an exit code, a recorded argv, a byte-exact string, a count, an ordering of events, or that something is gone, unchanged or exactly so many?
instructions.context: `claim` is what a task promises; `clauses` are its machine clauses, each with an id and its text. `probes` are the commands that prove it, each naming the clauses it proves; `legs` say which clause each part of the proof covers.

criteria.true: A program could decide it exactly
criteria.false: It needs a judgment to decide

instructions.question: Would at least one command in `probes` fail if `clauses[i].text` were false?
instructions.context: `clauses` are a task's machine clauses; `probes` are the commands that prove them, each with the clause ids it claims to prove (`proves`).

instructions.question: Does any entry of `legs` say something the clause it cites rules out?
instructions.context: `legs` are the proof's legs, each with its text and the clause ids it cites (`cites`); `clauses` are the task's machine clauses.

criteria.false: Every leg agrees with the clauses it cites

instructions.question: Does some file in `base` already pin the opposite of an entry of `clauses`, where that clause does not say the file changes?
instructions.context: `base` holds, for each file the task names, what it is at BASE: whether it exists, its line count, its headings or test names, and an `excerpt` of its lines carrying the task's literals. `clauses` are the task's machine clauses; asked only when `base` is present.

criteria.true: Some file at BASE already pins the opposite of a clause that does not say it changes
criteria.false: No file at BASE pins the opposite of a clause, or the clause says that file changes

authoring_link.rollback: skills/ultrawrite/stories/policy.json flag_at: flags off, the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Would `audience` expect this to happen: `link`?
instructions.context: `summary` says what the product is, why it exists and how it is used. `link` is a rule the app follows when something is deleted or changed.

criteria.false: It would surprise or upset them

authoring_routing.when: At plan_check.py --base, once per plan, for its ROUTING fact line
authoring_routing.rollback: risk unread: the branch is computed without it, and the line says so

instructions.question: Does `plan` change a high-stakes surface (auth, payments, migrations, data integrity, a public API, or loops, cursors, pagination, budgets or termination logic), or behaviour that is hard to verify by reading?
instructions.context: `plan` is an implementation plan: its tasks, each with its title, its claim (what it promises and the numbered machine clauses that restate it) and the files it touches.

criteria.true: It touches a high-stakes surface or behaviour hard to verify by reading
criteria.false: Every change is low-stakes and easy to verify by reading

authoring_desired_state.when: At check_provenance.py, once per quoted Claim whose issue resolves
authoring_desired_state.rollback: no reading: the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Does `sentence` say what should be true after the change, rather than what is wrong today?
instructions.context: `issue_body` is a GitHub issue's text; `sentence` is the sentence a plan quotes from it as its promise.

criteria.true: It says what should be true after the change
criteria.false: It describes what is wrong today

authoring_about_product.when: At jev_checks.ts --stage understanding, once per assumption the author labelled technical
authoring_about_product.rollback: flag off: the author's own read decides

instructions.question: Is `assumption` about what the app does, who uses it or how it looks?
instructions.context: `assumption` is something the author assumed while planning an app and labelled technical, a choice the person using the app would not see.

criteria.true: It is about what the app does, who uses it or how it looks
criteria.false: It is a technical choice the person using the app would never see
